questions.q: What is the formula to calculate the area of a rectangle if you are given its length and width?
questions.a: The formula is Area = length × width. A student who says "length + width" is confusing the formula for perimeter with area; they need to revisit the difference between boundary length and interior space.

questions.q: If you have a square with a side of 5 cm, why do we call the result "25 cm²" instead of just "25 cm"?
questions.a: We use cm² because area measures two-dimensional space, and we are multiplying centimeters by centimeters (cm × cm). An answer of "25 cm" reveals a misunderstanding that area is a length, rather than a measure of surface coverage.

questions.q: A rectangular garden is 8 meters long and 3 meters wide. How much space does it cover?
questions.a: 8 meters × 3 meters = 24 square meters (m²). A student who answers "22 meters" has likely calculated the perimeter [2 × (8 + 3)] instead of the area, showing they have not distinguished between walking around a shape and filling it.

questions.q: If a square has an area of 36 cm², what is the length of one of its sides?
questions.a: The side length is 6 cm, because 6 × 6 = 36. If a student answers "18" or "9," they are incorrectly dividing or guessing, showing they do not yet realize the area of a square is a number multiplied by itself.

questions.q: Can two different rectangles have the same area but different side lengths? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes. A rectangle of 4 cm × 3 cm has an area of 12 cm², and a rectangle of 6 cm × 2 cm also has an area of 12 cm². A student who says "no" thinks that area is tied to a specific set of dimensions, ignoring that different factors can produce the same product.

questions.q: Design a rectangle that has an area of 20 cm². What are the possible dimensions?
questions.a: Possible answers include 4 cm × 5 cm, 2 cm × 10 cm, or 1 cm × 20 cm. An answer that doesn't multiply to 20 shows a failure to grasp the relationship between dimensions and total area.
